title: Growing Together zoning and inclusionary zoning deferred
subtitle: Transit-area height and setback rules, affordable housing set-asides, heritage, amenity space and developer cost concerns drew many delegates.
overview: The Planning and Strategic Initiatives Committee held a long public meeting on two linked planning proposals: the Growing Together land use and zoning framework for seven protected major transit station areas, and a proposed inclusionary zoning policy that would require some affordable rental units in new developments. The meeting heard from roughly two dozen delegates and ran past 11 p.m.

The committee recommended deferring both items to the March 18, 2024 Special Council Meeting. The Growing Together deferral was {{vote:m1}} and the inclusionary zoning deferral was {{vote:m2}}. The aim is to give staff time to talk further with the people who made oral and written submissions. One councillor declared a conflict and took no part in either item.

For residents, nothing changes yet. The proposed rules on building heights, tower separation, amenity space and affordable housing are still open for discussion. Staff said both items must be finished by the end of the first quarter of 2024 because of the federal Housing Accelerator Fund agreement and the Official Plan update. Staff will report back on the submissions in March.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended deferring the Official Plan and zoning amendments for seven protected major transit station areas to the March 18, 2024 Special Council Meeting so staff can talk further with those who made submissions.

The committee recommended deferring the inclusionary zoning Official Plan and zoning amendments, and the memorandum of understanding with the Region of Waterloo, to March 18, 2024 so they can be considered alongside Growing Together.

debate: Many development-industry delegates said Growing Together's tower separation, setback and floor-plate rules would raise building costs and make some already-approved projects non-compliant. They asked for guidelines rather than fixed rules, and for some properties to be moved to higher zones such as SGA 4. Staff replied that the zones remove density caps and parking minimums, and that the rules were calibrated to buildings already approved.

A heritage delegate argued that SGA 2 and SGA 3 zoning inside heritage conservation districts would allow buildings far taller than the district plans support. Residents and other delegates asked for more time because of the Ward 10 vacancy during consultation. They also raised limited green space, parkland, loss of low-cost community space and access to sunlight.

Several delegates said they had too little time to respond after detailed rules were released in November. Staff said they had set up a process asking for ownership proof, a concept plan and a planning justification, and that some requests lacked this. One request, for Cedar and Madison Street lands, had staff support.

On inclusionary zoning, builders and home-builder groups said the January report changed market classifications and set-aside rates without enough consultation. They said costs would be passed to market-unit buyers and asked that rates be tied to land purchase date rather than building permit date. Staff said they met industry groups several times and that Growing Together's added permissions and fee exemptions offset the cost.

Councillors raised how eligibility would be monitored once tenants' incomes change, and whether a trigger could pause the policy if the market worsens. Staff said no legal way exists to move out tenants who later earn too much. Supporters of the policy noted the province allows 5 per cent affordable units now.
